status_summary: Executive Order 14159 (2025-01-20) directed State and DHS to use INA 243(d) sanctions to the fullest extent of the law. The main visible measures are entry proclamations under INA 212(f) and 215(a) rather than a formally cited 243(d) action: Proclamation 10949 (effective 2025-06-09) and Proclamation 10998 (effective 2026-01-01) fully suspend entry for 19 countries and partially suspend immigrant, B, F, M and J visas for 20 more, citing in part overstay rates and, for five countries, refusal to take back removable nationals; this design differs from the Mandate's country-specific 243(d) sanctions and goes beyond it in scope. State made a B-1/B-2 visa bond program permanent on 2026-08-03, and a final rule published 2026-03-11 (effective 2026-04-10, starting with DV-2027) requires Diversity Visa entrants to submit valid passport information; State also paused diversity visa issuance in December 2025, citing a review of screening and vetting. Two courts acted on related State pauses: on 2026-08-21 the Southern District of New York (CLINIC v. Rubio) vacated a 75-country immigrant visa pause on public-charge grounds, and on 2026-08-28 the Northern District of California (Medani v. Trump) temporarily vacated, pending further litigation, the diversity visa pause, the 75-country pause and a USCIS hold, after which a State notice updated 2026-08-31 says the December 2025 diversity visa pause is no longer in effect. Neither ruling addresses Proclamation 10998 or INA 243(d), and a secondary report of a February 2026 use of 243(d) against Cuban officials cites no government source.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14159, section 13, directed the Secretaries of State and Homeland Security to implement the sanctions authorized by INA 243(d) to the fullest extent allowed, to build acceptance of removable nationals into diplomatic negotiations, and to weigh a country's delays in verifying identities (published 2025-01-29).

Proclamation 10949 suspended entry for nationals of 12 countries and partially for 7 (immigrant visas plus B, F, M and J), effective 2025-06-09, citing among other things overstay rates and refusal to accept removable nationals (published 2025-06-10).
State published a temporary rule creating a visa bond pilot program for B-1/B-2 applicants from designated countries; the pilot ran from 2025-08-20 to 2026-08-05.

Proclamation 10998 expanded the restrictions effective 2026-01-01: 19 countries fully suspended and 20 partially suspended (by this tracker's count), plus holders of Palestinian Authority travel documents, and removed the broad family-member exception (published 2025-12-19).

A secondary immigration-news report says State used INA 243(d) to deny visas to eight senior Cuban baseball officials, citing Cuba's refusal of regular deportation flights (month-level date, first of month used; not confirmed from a State or DHS source).

State publishes a final rule (91 FR 11891, effective 2026-04-10, starting with DV-2027) requiring Diversity Visa entrants to provide valid passport information and a scan of the passport page, to confirm identities earlier, support vetting and curb fraudulent third-party entries.

State's final rule made the visa bond program permanent for B-1/B-2 applicants from State-designated countries, with bonds of $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000; country selection turns on overstay rates, information sharing and vetting weaknesses, and the rule does not list refusal to accept deportees as a criterion.

The Southern District of New York (Judge Jeannette Vargas, Catholic Legal Immigration Network v. Rubio, No. 26-cv-00858-JAV) grants plaintiffs partial summary judgment and vacates State's pause on immigrant visa issuance for nationals of 75 countries (announced 2026-01-14, effective 2026-01-21, implemented by a cable directing refusals under INA 221(g) on public-charge grounds). The court holds the policy contrary to law and beyond the Secretary's authority, including under the INA's nationality nondiscrimination provision, rejects a remand-only remedy, and does not address Proclamation 10998 or INA 243(d); news summaries say Proclamation 10998 was not affected.
timeline.source: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York

timeline.event: A law-firm blog reports that State told the court in CLINIC v. Rubio that it is complying with the judgment and that the 75-country pause is no longer in effect, and describes a separate, temporary worldwide pause on immigrant visa appointments through 2026-08-31 for consular training on a public-charge rule (court filings not linked).

The Northern District of California (Judge Edward J. Davila, Medani v. Trump, No. 5:26-cv-06332-EJD) temporarily vacates, pending further litigation, State's diversity visa issuance pause, State's 75-country immigrant visa pause and a USCIS adjustment hold, orders State to reconsider applications refused solely under those pauses and resume ordinary adjudication for the rest of FY2026, and certifies three subclasses of FY2026 selectees.

A State Department visa news notice (updated 2026-08-31) says that, as of 2026-08-28 and in line with the court's order in Medani v. Trump, the December 2025 pause on diversity visa issuance is no longer in effect.

title: Enforce visa reciprocity and INA 243(d) sanctions and review sensitive visa programs
uncertainties: No actual State or DHS invocation of INA 243(d) was verified; the Federal Register record of EO 14159 section 13 is the only primary document on 243(d), and the February 2026 use against Cuban officials comes from a secondary immigration-news site that cites no government source. Reciprocity-schedule changes and student-visa vetting changes were not researched, nor were court challenges to the proclamations. The 19 and 20 country counts are this tracker's tally from the proclamation text (Turkmenistan counted among the partial group; Laos and Sierra Leone moved from partial to full). The 75-country pause dates (announced 2026-01-14, effective 2026-01-21) come from the S.D.N.Y. opinion (mirror on media.nilc.org); State's 2026-08-28 filing in that case was not located, and the report that the pause ended rests on a law-firm blog. The State diversity visa notice, read through an automated summary, both says the December 2025 pause ended on 2026-08-28 and retains text announcing a pause on all diversity visa issuances (interviews continue, no visas issued) tied to a screening review; whether that text is the original December 2025 notice left on the page or a new pause was not resolved. The Medani order is a temporary vacatur with a joint status report due 2026-09-18; later proceedings were not checked. The December 2025 pause start date (a law firm gives 2025-12-23) was not confirmed on a State page.
